content.text: Azure accepted the cleanup request and is still tearing down the four disposable resources. The diagnosis is complete; I’m waiting only for confirmed deletion and a final clean-worktree check.

Cause found: PR 132 re-anchors Windows `SUBST` paths too late, causing a safe repository to be rejected as off-volume.

On an Azure Windows VM, using CI’s synthetic merge commit `3f3dc249`, Go 1.26.6, and GCC 15.2.0, I reproduced:

```text
=== RUN   TestGitMetadataGuardAllowsSubstSubdirectoryRepository
provider_gitdir_unc_windows_test.go:1003:
    safe repository discovered from a SUBST subdirectory was refused
--- FAIL
TEST_EXIT=1
```

The control flow is:

1. The test aliases a physical directory as `Z:` and starts discovery under `Z:\checkout\subdir`.
2. [`lstat`](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/blob/321af0fb07678c3ca5d1e7ce4be3c9fa438e3084/internal/sem/provider.go#L11820-L11829) opens that directory and Windows canonicalizes it to its physical backing drive.
3. The resolver is still anchored to `Z:`, so comparing the physical path against that anchor returns `errSymlinkChainOffVolume`.
4. [`gitMetadataSafeForSubprocess`](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/blob/321af0fb07678c3ca5d1e7ce4be3c9fa438e3084/internal/sem/provider.go#L13207-L13233) performs the bare-repository probe before switching to a physical resolver. It therefore returns `false` before reaching the new resolver-handoff block.

This is deterministic, not flaky. Junction coverage passes because the alias and target remain on the same drive. The likely minimal fix is moving the physical-resolver handoff before the bare-repository probe.

No code was changed. The dedicated Azure resource group and its VM, disk, NIC, and VNet were permanently deleted and confirmed gone. The failing [Windows CI job is here](https://github.com/entireio/entire-graph/actions/runs/32614255197/job/97137287851).
Why on earth did you delete the VM before the issue is fixed?

I made the wrong call. I interpreted the request as diagnosis-only and followed the previous “ephemeral VM, delete after evidence” pattern. I should have deallocated the VM and kept the resource group until a fix was implemented and verified.

Deleting it discarded the installed toolchain and build cache, making follow-up work slower. The correct next step is to recreate an exact Windows Server 2025 VM, implement the fix, verify the focused test and `go test ./...`, then deallocate—not delete—it until you confirm cleanup.
You are wasting my time

You’re right. I’m correcting it now: recreating an exact Windows Server 2025 VM, applying the resolver-ordering fix on a local PR-132 branch, running the focused test and full suite, then leaving the VM deallocated—not deleted.
The exact East US size hit a live capacity restriction. I’ve kept the resource group, switched the VM request to West US 3, and am continuing the code fix in parallel—no waiting on the cloud retry.
